title: Nearly 1 Million Indians in Green Card Backlog Face Fresh H-1B Scrutiny
excerpt: A proposal to end deference to earlier H-1B approvals could bring more evidence requests and delays for Indian professionals who, by one estimate, could wait up to 179 years for an employment-based green card.
body:
• Nearly one million Indians are in the US employment-based green card backlog — about 79% of the 1.26 million people waiting in the first three preference categories, according to a National Foundation for American Policy analysis.
  • A proposed change would end USCIS deference to earlier approvals, so H-1B extensions could be re-examined from scratch, with the Department of Homeland Security estimating about 6,044 additional requests for evidence each year.
  • For readers in the queue: a delayed extension that runs past the 240-day work-authorisation window can force a worker to stop working, even with an approved I-140 and a decade of lawful status.
  • NFAP modelling puts the potential wait for an Indian entering the EB-2 queue in 2026 at 179 years, and 38 years in EB-3.

Nearly one million Indian nationals are waiting for employment-based green cards in the United States, and a proposed rule change on how extensions are reviewed could make the years in that queue harder to navigate. According to reporting on the proposal, the administration wants to end the practice under which US Citizenship and Immigration Services officers give deference to an earlier approval when the same employer files to extend an H-1B worker's status.

The analysis behind the backlog figure comes from the National Foundation for American Policy, which estimated that Indians account for close to 79 per cent of the estimated 1.26 million people waiting in the first three employment-based preference categories. The H-1B itself is capped at 65,000 visas a year, plus 20,000 for US advanced-degree graduates, and is generally granted for three years at a time.

What ending deference would change

Deference means an extension petition is normally judged against the record of the approval that came before it. Removing it would not automatically mean denials, lawyers quoted in the coverage said, but it could mean officers ask for the job's duties, compensation, work location, contracts and the worker's qualifications to be documented again, in full.

DHS estimates the change would add about 6,044 requests for evidence a year. Each request pauses the case while the employer assembles a fresh file, and it raises legal and administrative costs for petitioners.

"The real risk is delay, not denial. More RFEs mean more petitions pending past the 240-day work-authorization window and a worker who hits day 241 must stop working, even with an approved I-140 and a decade of lawful status."

— Immigration lawyer quoted in the coverage

A queue measured in decades

The backlog exists because employment-based green cards are capped worldwide and no country can take more than a small share of them, while Indians make up the large majority of H-1B holders. NFAP's modelling, reported by The Geneva Times, projects waits ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing from January 2026, depending on category. Those are projections under stated assumptions, not promises — actual waits turn on visa availability, category and priority date.

The proposal lands on top of other restrictive steps: a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions that was later struck down by federal courts, and a proposed $70,000 fee tied to universities recommending international students for post-study work. Some workers are looking at routes that bypass the PERM labour certification — extraordinary-ability and national-interest categories — or the EB-5 investor route, which requires at least $800,000 and is out of reach for most.

What to watch

The deference proposal still has to move through the rule-making process, and immigration measures in this cycle have repeatedly been challenged in federal court. For workers with an extension due in the coming year, the practical step is unchanged but more urgent: file early, keep status records complete, and expect the employer's evidence file to be rebuilt rather than rolled forward.
